## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. The default recipe gives only 131072/(256×16) = 32 PPO updates. An exact build needs every one of about 6–16 placements to be right, so a policy that is only partly trained still scores 0. My main guess is that the number of updates and samples is the bottleneck. Halving ppo_epochs gives 1.86× the samples, and cutting n_envs to 64 gives about 4–7× as many updates. The second gap is in the head. It pools footprint features over the 2D grid but cannot check which layer a brick lands on against what the target holds at that layer. I propose two recipe-only trials that differ in epochs (1 vs 2) and one layer-aware head that uses recipe A, so it is cheap (r≈1.3).

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success in the last 10% of training. That holds across recipes with 1 epoch (408k samples), 2 epochs (232k samples) and a layer-aware head, so with 2 seeds each there is no signal to rank them. Changing the recipe alone did not help, so the next step is to change the architecture. The pooling head assumes the anchor is the brick's top-left corner and that pooling exactly over the footprint is right. The task warns that the world may differ from its description, and if it does, that fixed alignment could block learning. A placement head using a learned 3x3 convolution around each anchor makes no alignment assumption. A wider receptive field, or global attention, may also help with overhangs and placement order. One candidate also tests a longer horizon (gamma 0.99) with less entropy, which values the +1 exact-build bonus more.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev and on training (last 10%). That covers two recipes, a longer horizon, three head designs, and a CNN and a transformer trunk. When every result is 0, seed noise cannot explain it. Two explanations fit. First, the task may simply be too hard at this budget. Second, and I think more likely given the note about this world, the action index may not match the observation grid as described: it could be transposed, flipped, or in a different order. Every head so far ties each anchor's logit to nearby cells in the observation. If that alignment is wrong, the network cannot learn the task at all, even to the point of filling target cells. This round tests the alignment idea with heads that can learn which way the grid maps: (A) mirrored and transposed copies of the feature map, (B) a fully learned remapping of positions to actions, and (C) both together, plus the mask as an input.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0, and every one also had 0 training success. Changing the number of PPO epochs (1, 2 or 4) and the number of updates made no difference. Neither did the head type (footprint pooling, layer-aware pooling or a conv head), the trunk (CNN or transformer), or the tests for a mismatch between action index and grid (D4 views, a learned linear remap, the mask as input). So none of these is clearly the bottleneck, and the 2-seed noise tells us nothing here. One thing not yet isolated is the entropy bonus. It equals about 0.01 times ln(250), roughly 0.05 per step, which is about the size of the shaped reward for one correct placement (roughly 2 cells out of 30, or 0.07). That could keep the policy close to uniform. Two other things are also untested: normalisation and depth in the trunk, and a critic separate from the policy trunk. In this last round I test these three, and each also lowers entropy and uses a longer horizon.
